claim: Chronic itch affects millions of people worldwide.
source: Chronic itch is a debilitating disorder that affects millions of people worldwide (Matterne et al., 2011; Mollanazar et al., 2016; Dalgard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Matterne et al., 2011; Mollanazar et al., 2016; Dalgard et al., 2015).

claim: Chronic itch can be a disease in and of itself.
source: Like chronic pain, chronic itch can be a disease in and of itself (Ständer and Steinhoff, 2002; Oaklander, 2011; Dhand and Aminoff, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ständer and Steinhoff, 2002; Oaklander, 2011; Dhand and Aminoff, 2014).

claim: Persistent scratching in chronic itch disorders has no discernable benefit.
source: Unlike acute itch, which can facilitate removal of crawling insects, parasites, or irritants, persistent scratching in chronic itch disorders has no discernable benefit; scratching damages skin, leading to secondary infection, disfiguring lesions, and exacerbation of disease severity (Mollanazar et al., 2016; Yosipovitch and Papoiu, 2008; Ikoma et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mollanazar et al., 2016; Yosipovitch and Papoiu, 2008; Ikoma et al., 2006).

claim: Atopic dermatitis affects fifteen million people in the United States.
source: The most common chronic itch disorder is atopic dermatitis (AD; commonly known as eczema), which affects fifteen million people in the United States alone (Spergel and Paller, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Spergel and Paller, 2003).

claim: Severe AD can trigger the atopic march, where chronic itch and inflammation progress to food allergy, allergic rhinitis, and asthma.
source: Severe AD can trigger the atopic march, where chronic itch and inflammation progress to food allergy, allergic rhinitis, and asthma (Spergel and Paller, 2003; Zheng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Spergel and Paller, 2003; Zheng et al., 2011).

claim: A number of studies have identified biomarkers and disease genes in itchy human AD lesions.
source: A number of studies have identified biomarkers and disease genes in itchy human AD lesions (Ewald et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2012; Guttman-Yassky et al., 2009; Suárez-Fariñas et al., 2013; Jabbari et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ewald et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2012; Guttman-Yassky et al., 2009; Suárez-Fariñas et al., 2013; Jabbari et al., 2012).

claim: A recent study compared the transcriptomes of healthy skin to itchy and non-itchy skin from psoriasis and AD patients, revealing dramatic changes in expression of genes associated with cytokines, immune cells, epithelial cells, and sensory neurons.
source: Indeed, a recent study compared the transcriptomes of healthy skin to itchy and non-itchy skin from psoriasis and AD patients, revealing dramatic changes in expression of genes associated with cytokines, immune cells, epithelial cells, and sensory neurons (Nattkemper et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nattkemper et al., 2018).

claim: The MC903 mouse model of AD displays highly reproducible phenotypes that closely resemble human AD.
source: The MC903 model is ideal for our approach because of its highly reproducible phenotypes that closely resemble human AD and its ability to induce the development of lesions and scratching (Li et al., 2009; Li et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009; Oetjen et al., 2017; Morita et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2009; Li et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009; Oetjen et al., 2017; Morita et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2019).

claim: 62% of genes from a recent study of human chronic itch lesions were significantly changed for at least one of the time points examined in the MC903 model.
source: Overall, we found that 62% of genes from a recent study of human chronic itch lesions (Nattkemper et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and 67% of AD-related genes (Figure 1B) were significantly changed for at least one of the time points examined, suggesting that the MC903 mouse model recapitulates many key transcriptional changes occuring in human chronic itch and AD.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and citation to published literature (Nattkemper et al., 2018).

claim: 67% of AD-related genes were significantly changed for at least one of the time points examined in the MC903 model.
source: Overall, we found that 62% of genes from a recent study of human chronic itch lesions (Nattkemper et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and 67% of AD-related genes (Figure 1B) were significantly changed for at least one of the time points examined, suggesting that the MC903 mouse model recapitulates many key transcriptional changes occuring in human chronic itch and AD.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Proteases and skin barrier genes changed as early as six hours after the first MC903 treatment, before mice begin scratching.
source: In line with rapid changes in transcription, proteases (Klk6, Klk13, among others) and skin barrier genes (Cdhr1) changed as early as six hours after the first treatment, before mice begin scratching (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Increased protease activity in AD skin is thought to promote breakdown of the epidermal barrier and release of inflammatory cytokines from keratinocytes.
source: Increased protease activity in AD skin is thought to promote breakdown of the epidermal barrier and release of inflammatory cytokines from keratinocytes (Rattenholl and Steinhoff, 2003; Yosipovitch, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Rattenholl and Steinhoff, 2003; Yosipovitch, 2004).

claim: TSLP is a key inducer of the Type two immune response via signaling in CD4+ T cells, basophils, and other immune cells.
source: One such cytokine, thymic stromal lymphopoetin (TSLP) is a key inducer of the Type two immune response, which is characteristic of human AD and the MC903 model, via signaling in CD4+ T cells, basophils, and other immune cells (Li et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009; Briot et al., 2010; Demehri et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009; Briot et al., 2010; Demehri et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013).

claim: Beginning at day two, before any significant itch-evoked scratching, immune cell infiltration, or skin lesions were observed, increases in Tslp and several other epithelial-derived cytokines were seen.
source: Beginning at day two, before any significant itch-evoked scratching (Figure 1C), immune cell infiltration (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplements 3A, 4A and 5A–C), or skin lesions (data not shown) (Morita et al., 2015) were observed, we saw increases in Tslp, as well as several other epithelial-derived cytokines, including the neutrophil chemoattractant genes Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Cxcl3, and Cxcl5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D and behavioral/flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C, E-G.

claim: SLIGRL treatment of human keratinocytes triggered increased expression of several chemokine genes, including IL8 and CXCL2.
source: SLIGRL treatment triggered increased expression of several of these chemokine genes, including IL8, the human ortholog of mouse Cxcl1/Cxcl2, and CXCL2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Increased protease activity can rapidly trigger increases in neutrophil chemoattractants in skin.
source: These increases occurred after a few hours of exposure to SLIGRL, suggesting that increased protease activity can rapidly trigger increases in neutrophil chemoattractants in skin, similar to what we observe in MC903-treated mouse skin.
evidence: Inferred from SLIGRL treatment data in human keratinocytes and comparison to MC903 mouse model.

claim: Early changes in transcripts encoding neuronal outgrowth factors and axon pathfinding molecules were observed in skin prior to when mice began scratching.
source: Unexpectedly, in the skin we observed early changes in a number of transcripts encoding neuronal outgrowth factors (Ngf, Artn) and axon pathfinding molecules (Slit1, Sema3d, Sema3a), some of which are directly implicated in chronic itch (Hidaka et al., 2017; Kou et al., 2012; Tominaga and Takamori, 2013; Tominaga et al., 2007; Tominaga and Takamori, 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 7A), prior to when mice began scratching.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A and citations to published literature (Hidaka et al., 2017; Kou et al., 2012; Tominaga and Takamori, 2013; Tominaga et al., 2007; Tominaga and Takamori, 2014).

claim: Increased innervation of lesions was observed at day two but not day one of the MC903 model.
source: We saw increased innervation of lesions at day two but not day one of the model (Figure 1H–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 8A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 8A.

claim: An increase in CGRP+ innervation of skin was observed at day 2 of the MC903 model.
source: Indeed, we saw an increase in CGRP+ innervation of skin at day 2 (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 9A), which suggests that elevation of neuronal transcripts in skin is due to hyperinnervation of peptidergic itch and/or pain fibers.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 9A.

claim: Early hyperinnervation is promoted by local signaling in the skin and is independent of the itch-scratch cycle.
source: Our findings suggest that early hyperinnervation is promoted by local signaling in the skin and is independent of the itch-scratch cycle.
evidence: Inferred from observation that hyperinnervation occurs before scratching behaviors begin.

claim: By day five, mice exhibited robust itch behaviors and stark changes in a number of AD disease genes.
source: By day five, mice exhibited robust itch behaviors (Figure 1C) and stark changes in a number of AD disease genes (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Flg2 levels sharply decreased at day five of the MC903 model.
source: Interestingly, Flg2 levels sharply decreased at day five.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Neutrophils were the most abundant immune cell subtype in skin at day 5 of the MC903 model.
source: Using flow cytometry, we observed a number of infiltrating immune cells in the skin at day 5. Of these, we neutrophils were the most abundant immune cell subtype (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: At day eight of the MC903 model, the classical AD-associated immune signature was observed in the skin, with upregulation of Il4, Il33 and other Th2-associated genes.
source: It was not until day eight that we observed the classical AD-associated immune signature in the skin, (Gittler et al., 2012) with upregulation of Il4, Il33 and other Th2-associated genes (Figure 1B, Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and 1D, and citation to published literature (Gittler et al., 2012).

claim: Increases in the T cell chemoattractant genes Cxcl9, Cxcl10, and Cxcl11 were observed at day eight of the MC903 model.
source: We also observed increases in the T cell chemoattractant genes Cxcl9, Cxcl10, and Cxcl11 (Figure 1D), which are thought to be hallmarks of chronic AD lesions in humans (Oetjen and Kim, 2018; Mansouri and Guttman-Yassky, 2015).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D and citations to published literature (Oetjen and Kim, 2018; Mansouri and Guttman-Yassky, 2015).

claim: Neutrophils and several other immune cells were robustly elevated in skin by day eight of the MC903 model, including basophils, CD4+ T cells, eosinophils, and mast cells.
source: Neutrophils and a number of other immune cells that started to infiltrate on day five were robustly elevated in skin by day eight, including basophils (Figure 1F), CD4+ T cells (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), eosinophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C), and mast cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), but not inflammatory monocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F, 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-C.

claim: CD4+ T cells play a key role in IL4Rα-dependent sensitization of pruriceptors in the second week of the MC903 model.
source: More specifically, they play a key role in IL4Rα-dependent sensitization of pruriceptors in the second week of the MC903 model (Oetjen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Oetjen et al., 2017).

claim: Itch behaviors preceded significant CD4+ T cell infiltration in the MC903 model.
source: Thus, we were quite surprised to find that itch behaviors preceded significant CD4+ T cell infiltration.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of behavioral data (Figure 1C) and flow cytometry data (Figure 1G).

claim: Neutrophils release known pruritogens, including proteases, reactive oxygen species, and/or histamine, inflammatory lipids, and cytokines that sensitize and/or activate pruriceptors.
source: Moreover, neutrophils release known pruritogens, including proteases, reactive oxygen species, and/or histamine, inflammatory lipids, and cytokines that sensitize and/or activate pruriceptors (Dong and Dong, 2018; Hashimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dong and Dong, 2018; Hashimoto et al., 2018).

claim: Increased levels of the prostaglandin PGE2 and the neutrophil-specific leukotriene LTB4 have been reported in skin of AD patients.
source: Increased levels of the prostaglandin PGE2 and the neutrophil-specific leukotriene LTB4 have also been reported in skin of AD patients (Fogh et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Fogh et al., 1989).

claim: Increases in several inflammatory lipids, PGD2 and PGE2, as well as LTB4 and its precursor 5-HETE, were observed in MC903-treated skin by mass spectrometry.
source: Indeed, by mass spectrometry, we observed increases in several of these inflammatory lipids, PGD2 and PGE2, as well as LTB4 and its precursor 5-HETE (Figure 1—figure supplement 10A) in MC903-treated skin, implicating neutrophils in driving AD itch and inflammation.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10A.

claim: Systemic depletion of neutrophils using daily injections of an anti-Gr1 antibody dramatically attenuated itch-evoked scratching through the first eight days of the MC903 model.
source: Systemic depletion of neutrophils using daily injections of an anti-Gr1 (aGr1) antibody (Ghasemlou et al., 2015; Sivick et al., 2014) dramatically attenuated itch-evoked scratching through the first eight days of the model (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and citations to published literature (Ghasemlou et al., 2015; Sivick et al., 2014).

claim: The neutrophil depletion strategy significantly and selectively reduced circulating and skin infiltrating neutrophils on days five and eight of the MC903 model.
source: Consistent with a key role for neutrophils in driving chronic itch, our depletion strategy significantly and selectively reduced circulating and skin infiltrating neutrophils on days five and eight, days on which control, but not depleted mice, scratched robustly (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Basophils and CD4+ T cells continued to infiltrate the skin following aGr1 treatment.
source: In contrast, basophils and CD4+ T cells continued to infiltrate the skin following aGr1 treatment (Figure 2C–D), suggesting that these cells are not required for early MC903 itch.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: CXCL1 injection triggered significant and selective recruitment of neutrophils to cheek skin within 15 min.
source: As expected, we observed significant and selective recruitment of neutrophils to cheek skin within 15 min after CXCL1 injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: CXCL1 injection triggered robust scratching behaviors.
source: CXCL1 injection also triggered robust scratching behaviors (Figure 2E) on a similar time course to neutrophil infiltration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2E and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: aGr1-treatment rapidly reduced circulating neutrophils and resulted in a dramatic loss of CXCL1-evoked itch behaviors.
source: Indeed, aGr1-treatment rapidly reduced circulating neutrophils (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and resulted in a dramatic loss of CXCL1-evoked itch behaviors (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Injection of chloroquine still triggered robust scratching in aGr1-treated animals.
source: This effect was specific to neutrophil-induced itch, as injection of chloroquine, a pruritogen that directly activates pruriceptors to trigger itch, still triggered robust scratching in aGr1-treated animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: CXCL1-mediated neutrophil infiltration is sufficient to drive acute itch behaviors.
source: However, our results show that CXCL1-mediated neutrophil infiltration is sufficient to drive acute itch behaviors, and that neutrophils are necessary for itch in the MC903 model.
evidence: Inferred from CXCL1 injection and neutrophil depletion experiments.

claim: Neutrophils are necessary for itch in the MC903 model.
source: However, our results show that CXCL1-mediated neutrophil infiltration is sufficient to drive acute itch behaviors, and that neutrophils are necessary for itch in the MC903 model.
evidence: Supported by neutrophil depletion experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MC903-treated TSLPR KO mice displayed robust scratching behaviors through the first eight days of the model.
source: Surprisingly, MC903-treated TSLPR KO mice displayed robust scratching behaviors through the first eight days of the model (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TSLPR KO mice displayed robust neutrophil infiltration.
source: In contrast to our results in aGr1-injected mice, TSLPR KO mice displayed robust neutrophil infiltration (Figure 2G), but completely lacked basophil and CD4+ T cell infiltration into the skin (Figure 2H–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), and additionally displayed a reduction in mast cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: TSLPR KO mice completely lacked basophil and CD4+ T cell infiltration into the skin.
source: In contrast to our results in aGr1-injected mice, TSLPR KO mice displayed robust neutrophil infiltration (Figure 2G), but completely lacked basophil and CD4+ T cell infiltration into the skin (Figure 2H–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), and additionally displayed a reduction in mast cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2H-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Basophils and CD4+ T cells are not required for early itch in the MC903 model.
source: These results suggest that basophils and CD4+ T cells are not required for early itch and further support an inciting role for neutrophils.
evidence: Inferred from TSLPR KO mouse data showing robust itch despite lack of basophils and CD4+ T cells.

claim: A significant reduction in itch-evoked scratching was observed in TSLPR KO mice in the second week of the MC903 model.
source: Consistent with a later role for TSLP signaling in AD, we did observe a significant reduction in itch-evoked scratching in TSLPR KO mice in the second week of the model (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Neutrophils are necessary for initiation of AD and itch behaviors early in the development of AD, whereas TSLPR signaling mediates the recruitment of basophils and CD4+ T cells to promote later stage itch and chronic inflammation.
source: Thus, our data support a model in which neutrophils are necessary for initiation of AD and itch behaviors early in the development of AD, whereas TSLPR signaling mediates the recruitment of basophils and CD4+ T cells to promote later stage itch and chronic inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from neutrophil depletion and TSLPR KO experiments showing differential roles at different time points.

claim: Neutrophil depletion in the second week with aGr1 robustly decreased skin-infiltrating neutrophils and substantially reduced scratching behaviors at day 12.
source: Neutrophil depletion in the second week with aGr1 robustly decreased skin-infiltrating neutrophils (Figure 2J), and substantially reduced scratching behaviors at day 12 (Figure 2K), supporting a role for neutrophils in chronic itch.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2J and behavioral data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: A 79% mean reduction in time spent scratching was observed after neutrophil depletion at day 12, whereas loss of TSLPR effected a 44% reduction in time spent scratching.
source: Interestingly, we observed a 79% mean reduction in time spent scratching after neutrophil depletion at day 12, whereas loss of TSLPR effected a 44% reduction in time spent scratching.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from neutrophil depletion and TSLPR KO experiments.

claim: Neutrophils infiltrated DNFB- but not vehicle-treated skin.
source: Indeed, neutrophils also infiltrated DNFB- but not vehicle-treated skin (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Only 84 genes were differentially expressed in trigeminal ganglia through the eighth day of the MC903 model.
source: In contrast to the skin, where we saw many early transcriptional changes, we did not see any significant transcriptional changes in the trigeminal ganglia (TG) until five days after the first treatment, and in total only 84 genes were differentially expressed through the eighth day (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Enrichment of neuronal markers expressed by NP3 neurons was observed in trigeminal ganglia.
source: Interestingly, we observed enrichment of neuronal markers expressed by one specific subset of somatosensory neurons that are dedicated to itch (Il31ra, Osmr, Trpa1, Cysltr2, and Nppb), termed 'NP3' neurons (Dong and Dong, 2018; Usoskin et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018; Solinski et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citations to published literature (Dong and Dong, 2018; Usoskin et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018; Solinski et al., 2019b).

claim: Changes in neuroinflammatory and immune genes occurred just a few days after itch onset in the MC903 model.
source: Similar to what has been reported in mouse models of chronic pain, we observed changes in neuroinflammatory (Bdnf, Nptx1, Nptx2, Nptxr) and immune genes (Itk, Cd19, Rag, Tmem173). However, these transcriptional changes occurred just a few days after itch onset, in contrast to the slow changes in nerve injury and pain models that occur over weeks, indicating that neuropathic changes may occur sooner than previously thought in chronic itch.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and comparison to chronic pain models.

claim: A significant increase in TG immune cell counts was observed at day eight but not day five of the MC903 model.
source: We observed a significant increase in TG immune cell counts at day eight but not day five (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Upregulation of Lcn2 occurred on day eight of the MC903 model.
source: Surprisingly, we saw upregulation of Lcn2 on day eight of the MC903 model and, additionally, we observed robust induction of immediate early genes (Fos, Junb, Figure 3G), suggesting that MC903 itch drives activity-dependent changes in the spinal cord as early as one week after beginning treatment.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Robust induction of immediate early genes (Fos, Junb) was observed in spinal cord on day eight of the MC903 model.
source: Surprisingly, we saw upregulation of Lcn2 on day eight of the MC903 model and, additionally, we observed robust induction of immediate early genes (Fos, Junb, Figure 3G), suggesting that MC903 itch drives activity-dependent changes in the spinal cord as early as one week after beginning treatment.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: MC903 itch drives activity-dependent changes in the spinal cord as early as one week after beginning treatment.
source: Surprisingly, we saw upregulation of Lcn2 on day eight of the MC903 model and, additionally, we observed robust induction of immediate early genes (Fos, Junb, Figure 3G), suggesting that MC903 itch drives activity-dependent changes in the spinal cord as early as one week after beginning treatment.
evidence: Inferred from observation of Lcn2 and immediate early gene upregulation in spinal cord.

claim: Sustained itch and inflammation can drive changes in the PNS and CNS within days rather than weeks after the onset of scratching.
source: Together, our findings show that sustained itch and inflammation can drive changes in the PNS and CNS much sooner than previously thought, within days rather than weeks after the onset of scratching.
evidence: Inferred from rapid transcriptional changes observed in trigeminal ganglia and spinal cord.

claim: Il33 upregulation is both neutrophil- and TSLPR-dependent.
source: For example, Il33 upregulation is both neutrophil- and TSLPR-dependent (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upregulation of epithelial-derived cytokines and chemokines Tslp, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Cxcl3, and Cxcl5 was unaffected by either loss of TSLPR or neutrophil depletion.
source: By contrast, upregulation of epithelial-derived cytokines and chemokines Tslp, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Cxcl3, and Cxcl5 was unaffected by either loss of TSLPR or neutrophil depletion (Figure 4B), suggesting these molecules are produced by skin cells even when the MC903-evoked immune response is compromised.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Il4 upregulation was completely dependent on TSLPR but not neutrophils.
source: Consistent with previous studies, Il4 upregulation was completely dependent on TSLPR but not neutrophils, establishing a role for TSLP signaling in the Type two immune response.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and consistency with previous studies.

claim: Cxcl10 expression was increased in TSLPR KO but not neutrophil-depleted skin.
source: One such gene was Cxcl10, a chemokine known to be released by skin epithelial cells, neutrophils, and other myeloid cells (Hashimoto et al., 2018; Ioannidis et al., 2016; Kanda et al., 2007; Koga et al., 2008; Michalec et al., 2002; Padovan et al., 2002; Tamassia et al., 2007).Cxcl10 expression was increased in TSLPR KO but not neutrophil-depleted skin (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and citations to published literature (Hashimoto et al., 2018; Ioannidis et al., 2016; Kanda et al., 2007; Koga et al., 2008; Michalec et al., 2002; Padovan et al., 2002; Tamassia et al., 2007).

claim: CXCL10 has been previously shown to drive acute itch in a model of allergic contact dermatitis via CXCR3 signaling in sensory neurons.
source: CXCL10 has been previously shown to drive acute itch in a model of allergic contact dermatitis via CXCR3 signaling in sensory neurons, (Qu et al., 2015) and is elevated in skin of AD patients (Mansouri and Guttman-Yassky, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Qu et al., 2015; Mansouri and Guttman-Yassky, 2015).

claim: Expression of Cxcl9 and Cxcl11 was decreased in AD skin of neutrophil-depleted mice.
source: Expression of Cxcl9 and Cxcl11, two other CXCR3 ligands that are elevated in AD but have an unknown role in itch, was also decreased in AD skin of neutrophil-depleted mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neutrophil depletion attenuated the expression of activity-induced immediate early genes (Vgf, Junb) in the TG.
source: Consistent with this model, neutrophil depletion attenuated the expression of activity-induced immediate early genes (Vgf, Junb) in the TG, suggestive of neutrophil-dependent sensory neuronal activity (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of Lcn2 and activity-induced genes Fos and Junb were not increased in spinal cord isolated from neutrophil-depleted animals.
source: For example, we observed that expression of Lcn2, a marker of neuropathic itch, and activity-induced genes Fos and Junb were not increased in spinal cord isolated from neutrophil-depleted animals, indicating that neutrophil-dependent scratching behaviors may indeed drive changes in the CNS (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neutrophil-depleted animals displayed no skin hyperinnervation at day two.
source: We also observed that neutrophil-depleted animals displayed no skin hyperinnervation at day two (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Low numbers of skin neutrophils are sufficient to mediate early hyperinnervation effects.
source: This result was surprising because we did not observe significant neutrophil infiltration at this early time point, but these data suggest that low numbers of skin neutrophils are sufficient to mediate these early effects.
evidence: Inferred from observation that hyperinnervation is neutrophil-dependent despite low neutrophil numbers at day 2.

claim: CXCL10 protein was increased in MC903-treated skin from uninjected wild-type and TSLPR KO animals, but not in skin from neutrophil-depleted mice.
source: We performed ELISA on cheek skin homogenate and found that CXCL10 protein was increased in MC903-treated skin from uninjected wild-type and TSLPR KO animals, but not in skin from neutrophil-depleted mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The CXCR3 antagonist strongly attenuated scratching behaviors on days five, eight, and twelve of the MC903 model.
source: We found that the CXCR3 antagonist strongly attenuated scratching behaviors on days five, eight, and twelve (Figure 4G), with the greatest effect at day eight.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CXCR3 blockade did not attenuate scratching behaviors in naive mice injected with the pruritogen chloroquine.
source: In contrast, CXCR3 blockade did not attenuate scratching behaviors in naive mice injected with the pruritogen chloroquine (Figure 4G), demonstrating that CXCR3 signaling contributes to chronic itch but is not required for scratching in response to an acute pruritogen.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Neutrophils promote chronic itch in atopic dermatitis via upregulation of CXCL10 and subsequent activation of CXCR3-dependent itch pathways.
source: Thus, we propose that neutrophils promote chronic itch in atopic dermatitis via upregulation of CXCL10 and subsequent activation of CXCR3-dependent itch pathways (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from neutrophil depletion, CXCL10 ELISA, and CXCR3 antagonism experiments.

claim: Neutrophils are essential for the early development of MC903-evoked itch.
source: Here, we show that neutrophils are essential for the early development of MC903-evoked itch.
evidence: Supported by neutrophil depletion experiments.

claim: The recruitment of neutrophils to the skin is sufficient to drive itch behaviors within minutes of infiltration.
source: We further show that the recruitment of neutrophils to the skin is sufficient to drive itch behaviors within minutes of infiltration.
evidence: Supported by CXCL1 injection experiments.

claim: Only a few studies have reported the presence of neutrophils in human AD lesions.
source: Only a few studies have even reported the presence of neutrophils in human AD lesions (Choy et al., 2012; Koro et al., 1999; Mihm et al., 1976; Shalit et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Choy et al., 2012; Koro et al., 1999; Mihm et al., 1976; Shalit et al., 1987).

claim: Neutrophils have been implicated in psoriatic inflammation and inflammatory pain.
source: Neutrophils have been implicated in psoriatic inflammation and inflammatory pain, (Sumida et al., 2014; Perkins and Tracey, 2000; Guerrero et al., 2008; Cunha et al., 2003; Finley et al., 2013; Carreira et al., 2013; Levine et al., 2006; Schön et al., 2000) where they are thought to rapidly respond to tissue injury and inflammation, (Oyoshi et al., 2012) but they have not been directly linked to itch.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Sumida et al., 2014; Perkins and Tracey, 2000; Guerrero et al., 2008; Cunha et al., 2003; Finley et al., 2013; Carreira et al., 2013; Levine et al., 2006; Schön et al., 2000; Oyoshi et al., 2012).

claim: In allergy, mast cells infiltrate the upper dermis and epidermis and release pruritogens to cause itch.
source: In allergy, mast cells infiltrate the upper dermis and epidermis and release pruritogens to cause itch, (Solinski et al., 2019b; Meixiong et al., 2019) whereas in tissue injury, mast cell activation can trigger pain hypersensitivity (Chatterjea and Martinov, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Solinski et al., 2019b; Meixiong et al., 2019; Chatterjea and Martinov, 2015).

claim: In pyoderma gangrenosum, neutrophils are recruited to the deep dermal layers to promote tissue damage and pain.
source: For example, pyoderma gangrenosum, which causes painful skin ulcerations recruits neutrophils to the deep dermal layers to promote tissue damage and pain (Hashimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hashimoto et al., 2018).

claim: In AD, neutrophils are recruited to the upper dermis and epidermis.
source: In AD, neutrophils are recruited to the upper dermis and epidermis, (Choy et al., 2012; Shalit et al., 1987) and we now show that neutrophils trigger itch in AD.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Choy et al., 2012; Shalit et al., 1987) and data from this study.

claim: Neutrophils recruited to subcutaneous sites during invasive streptococcal infection alleviate pain by clearing the tissue of bacteria.
source: Adding to the complex and diverse roles of neutrophils, neutrophils recruited to subcutaneous sites during invasive streptococcal infection alleviate pain by clearing the tissue of bacteria (Pinho-Ribeiro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Pinho-Ribeiro et al., 2018).

claim: TSLP signaling and the Type two immune response play an important role in the development of itch in the second week of the MC903 model.
source: In addition to neutrophils, TSLP signaling and the Type two immune response plays an important role in the development of itch in the second week of the MC903 model.
evidence: Supported by TSLPR KO mouse data.

claim: Neutrophils play an early role in triggering itch and also contribute to chronic itch in parallel with the TSLP-Type two response.
source: We propose that neutrophils play an early role in triggering itch and also contribute to chronic itch in parallel with the TSLP-Type two response.
evidence: Inferred from neutrophil depletion experiments at different time points and TSLPR KO data.

claim: Induction of Cxcl9/10/11 genes was completely dependent on neutrophils.
source: One of the few exceptions were the Th1-associated genes Cxcl9/10/11 (Ewald et al., 2017; Brunner et al., 2017). We found that induction of these genes and of CXCL10 protein was completely dependent on neutrophils.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and ELISA data, and citations to published literature (Ewald et al., 2017; Brunner et al., 2017).

claim: Depletion of neutrophils in the second week of the MC903 model can attenuate chronic itch-evoked scratching.
source: Moreover, we also demonstrate that depletion of neutrophils in the second week of the MC903 model can attenuate chronic itch-evoked scratching.
evidence: Supported by neutrophil depletion experiments on days 8-11.

claim: Several studies report that neutrophils and/or neutrophil chemokines are present in chronic lesions of human and mouse models of AD and related chronic itch disorders.
source: In examining previous characterizations of both human and mouse models of AD and related chronic itch disorders, several studies report that neutrophils and/or neutrophil chemokines are indeed present in chronic lesions (Ewald et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2012; Guttman-Yassky et al., 2009; Suárez-Fariñas et al., 2013; Jabbari et al., 2012; Nattkemper et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Saunders et al., 2016; Andersson, 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Malik et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ewald et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2012; Guttman-Yassky et al., 2009; Suárez-Fariñas et al., 2013; Jabbari et al., 2012; Nattkemper et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Saunders et al., 2016; Andersson, 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Malik et al., 2017).

claim: Neutrophils set the stage for the acute-to-chronic itch transition by triggering molecular changes necessary to develop a chronic, itchy lesion.
source: Our observations newly implicate neutrophils in setting the stage for the acute-to-chronic itch transition by triggering molecular changes necessary to develop a chronic, itchy lesion and also contributing to persistent itch.
evidence: Inferred from neutrophil depletion experiments showing effects on gene expression and itch behaviors.

claim: The CXCR3 ligand CXCL10 contributes to mouse models of acute and allergic itch.
source: The CXCR3 ligand CXCL10 contributes to mouse models of acute and allergic itch (Qu et al., 2015; Qu et al., 2017; Jing et al., 2018); however, its role in chronic itch was previously unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Qu et al., 2015; Qu et al., 2017; Jing et al., 2018).

claim: Dupilumab does not significantly reduce CXCL10 protein levels in human AD lesions.
source: Our observations are in alignment with a recent study showing that dupilumab, a new AD drug that blocks IL4Rα, a major downstream effector of the TSLP signaling pathway, does not significantly reduce CXCL10 protein levels in human AD lesions (Hamilton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hamilton et al., 2014).

claim: The TSLP/IL-4 and neutrophil/CXCL10 pathways are not highly interdependent.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the TSLP/IL-4 and neutrophil/CXCL10 pathways are not highly interdependent, and supports our findings that Il4 transcript is robustly upregulated in the absence of neutrophils.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq data showing Il4 upregulation in neutrophil-depleted mice and literature on dupilumab effects.

claim: Targeting IL4Rα signaling has been successful in treating itch and inflammation in some, but not all, AD patients.
source: Additionally, targeting IL4Rα signaling has been successful in treating itch and inflammation in some, but not all, AD patients (Simpson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Simpson et al., 2016).

claim: Biologics or compounds targeting neutrophils and/or the CXCR3 pathway may be useful for AD that is incompletely cleared by dupilumab monotherapy.
source: We propose that biologics or compounds targeting neutrophils and/or the CXCR3 pathway may be useful for AD that is incompletely cleared by dupilumab monotherapy.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on findings that neutrophils and CXCR3 contribute to itch independently of TSLP/IL-4 pathway.

claim: MDX-1100, a biologic that targets CXCL10, has shown efficacy for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis in phase II clinical trials.
source: For example, MDX-1100, a biologic that targets CXCL10, has already shown efficacy for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis in phase II clinical trials (Yellin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Yellin et al., 2012).

claim: CXCL10 or CXCR3 may be promising targets for treating chronic itch.
source: While rheumatoid arthritis and AD have distinct etiologies, (Scott et al., 2010) our body of work indicates that CXCL10 or CXCR3 may be promising targets for treating chronic itch.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on CXCR3 antagonism data and citation to published literature (Scott et al., 2010).

claim: Neutrophils incite itch and inflammation in early AD through directly triggering itch upon infiltration into the skin and indirectly triggering itch by altering expression of endogenous pruritogens.
source: Overall, our data suggest that neutrophils incite itch and inflammation in early AD through several mechanisms, including: 1) directly triggering itch upon infiltration into the skin, as shown by acute injection of CXCL1, and, 2) indirectly triggering itch by altering expression of endogenous pruritogens (e.g. induction of Cxcl10 expression; Hashimoto et al., 2018; Ioannidis et al., 2016; Kanda et al., 2007; Koga et al., 2008; Michalec et al., 2002; Padovan et al., 2002; Tamassia et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from CXCL1 injection, neutrophil depletion, and CXCL10 data, with citations to published literature (Hashimoto et al., 2018; Ioannidis et al., 2016; Kanda et al., 2007; Koga et al., 2008; Michalec et al., 2002; Padovan et al., 2002; Tamassia et al., 2007).

claim: MC903 treatment may model filaggrin loss-of-function mutations, which are a key inciting factor in human heritable atopic disease.
source: For example, we provide evidence that MC903 treatment may also model the filaggrin loss-of-function mutations, which are a key inciting factor in human heritable atopic disease (Palmer et al., 2006; Sandilands et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from observation of Flg2 downregulation in MC903 model and citations to published literature (Palmer et al., 2006; Sandilands et al., 2007).

claim: The MC903 model recapitulates several hallmarks of neuropathic disease on a time course much shorter than has been reported for chronic itch or chronic pain.
source: Furthermore, we have mapped the time course of gene expression changes in primary sensory ganglia and spinal cord during chronic itch development. We show that the MC903 model recapitulates several hallmarks of neuropathic disease on a time course much shorter than has been reported for chronic itch, or chronic pain.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from trigeminal ganglia and spinal cord.
